**Inputs:** A set of original 3D Gaussians (leaves), camera position $\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}$, and a global LoD threshold $T$.
**Outputs:** A cut set of nodes to render.
- **Non-leaf nodes:** Approximate their children.
Each node $i$ has a mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i$ and a scale metric $s_i^j$.
- **Tree Layout:** Implicit or explicit parent-child pointers.
Initialize an empty cut set $\mathcal{C}$.
Perform a Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from the root node.
Evaluate the cut condition $c_{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam})$.
Skip processing all children of node $i$.
If false, continue BFS to process children of node $i$.
- $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i$ is the mean position of node $i$.
- $\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}}$ is the camera position.
- $T$ is a global LoD threshold parameter.
- $s_i^j$ represents the scale components of node $i$.
Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it controls the granularity of the hierarchy.
- **Degenerate Input:** If a node has no children (leaf), the condition is evaluated against the leaf's properties.
This strategy determines how nearby Gaussians are merged into non-leaf nodes.
It is a prerequisite for building the hierarchy tree.
**Time Complexity:** The BFS traversal is linear with respect to the number of nodes in the hierarchy.
The cut condition evaluation is constant time per node.

**Memory Complexity:** The hierarchy structure adds overhead for parent-child pointers and aggregated node properties, but allows for significant reduction in the number of Gaussians rendered per frame by skipping distant subtrees.
With hierarchy, ultra-large scale reconstructions become feasible.
**Strengths:** View-adaptive LoD, efficient memory usage for large scenes.
**Limitations:** Requires hierarchical construction; performance depends on the quality of the cut condition and tree balance.
It enables real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale reconstructions by leveraging external memory and hierarchical culling.
